candidate.answerReason: The sum of the two distances is at least 1, attaining 1 throughout [3,4]. Consequently the strict inequality is possible exactly when a>1.

methods.label: Interpret the absolute values as distances
methods.explanation:
The quantities \(|x-3|\) and \(|x-4|\) are the distances from \(x\) to \(3\) and \(4\) on the number line. Traveling from \(3\) to \(x\) and then to \(4\) cannot be shorter than the direct distance from \(3\) to \(4\), which is \(1\). Thus
\[
|x-4|+|x-3|\ge 1.
\]
Equality holds exactly when \(3\le x\le4\). The given strict inequality therefore implies
\[
1\le |x-4|+|x-3|<a,
\]
so \(a>1\). Conversely, every \(a>1\) permits \(x=3\), for which the sum equals \(1<a\). Hence the condition is exactly \(a>1\), choice E.
methods.levelReason: Uses elementary number-line distances and the shortest-segment principle.

methods.label: Split at the sign changes
methods.explanation:
The expressions inside the absolute values change sign at \(3\) and \(4\). Splitting there gives all possible real values of \(x\):
\[
|x-4|+|x-3|=
\begin{cases}
7-2x>1,&x<3,\\
1,&3\le x\le4,\\
2x-7>1,&x>4.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus the minimum sum is \(1\), attained on the entire closed interval \([3,4]\). Since the problem requires the sum to be strictly less than \(a\), no \(a\le1\) can work. Every \(a>1\) does work by choosing \(x=3\). Therefore \(a>1\), choice E.
methods.levelReason: Uses the elementary sign rule for absolute values and three exhaustive intervals.
